en: The Questions of King Milinda:
The Introductory Discourse 1.
The Previous Connection, etc.
"Previous connection" (*pubbayoga*) refers to their past karma.
It is said that in the past, while the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa was current, a great community of monks resided in a monastery near the Ganges.
There, monks endowed with proper conduct and virtue would rise early in the morning, take up their brooms and dustpans, and—
While recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, they swept the courtyard and gathered the refuse into a heap.
Then one bhikkhu said to a novice, “Come, novice, throw away this refuse,” but he walked on as if not hearing him; he spoke a second time…
Even when addressed for a third time, he continued on his way as if not hearing him at all.
Then that bhikkhu, thinking, "This novice is indeed difficult to speak with," became angry and struck him with the broom-handle.
Thereupon, weeping and casting away the refuse out of fear, he thought: "By this meritorious deed of clearing away refuse, until I..."
"May I attain Nibbāna; until then, in whatever place I am reborn, may I be of great influence and great power, like the midday sun"—
thus he made his first aspiration.
Having discarded his refuse, he went to the Ganges ford to bathe; seeing the surge of the Ganges' waves roaring, he made this aspiration:
"Until I attain Nibbāna, in every place where I am reborn during this interval, may I possess spontaneous presence of mind like this surge of waves—an inexhaustible eloquence."
A second time he made an aspiration.
That monk, having set aside his broom in the broom-house and going to the Ganges ford to bathe, heard the novice’s aspiration and thought:
“If even one who was employed by me makes such an aspiration, why should it not succeed for me?”
Having reflected thus: "Until I reach Nibbāna, in every place where I am reborn during this interval, may I possess inexhaustible eloquence like this surge of the Ganges;
may I be capable of disentangling and resolving every question and its answer as it is asked."
He established his aspiration.
Both of them, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, passed an entire interval between Buddhas.
Then, just as our Blessed One saw the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, so too did he see these two.
It is indicated that five hundred years after my final nibbāna these [teachers] will arise; they will,
by means of questioning, similes, and logical reasoning, unravel and clarify the Dhamma and Vinaya which I have taught with subtle precision.
Among them, in Jambudīpa, in the city of Sāgala, there was a king named Milinda.

He was wise, competent, intelligent, and capable in the application of mantras, rituals, and practices pertaining to the past, future, and present; he acted with deliberation at the time of performing them, and many scriptures had been mastered by him.
Namely:
Grammar, conventional usage, arithmetic, logic, ethics, erotics, music, medicine, the four Vedas, the Purāṇas, histories, astrology,
sorcery, flags, incantations, warfare, prosody, and the word of the Buddha— these nineteen [sciences] he mastered. A debater,
difficult to approach and difficult to overcome, he was declared the foremost among the various founders of sects throughout the whole of Jambudvīpa by King Milinda.
There was no one equal to him in strength, speed, valor, and wisdom; he was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with an infinite army and transport.
Then one day, King Milinda, desiring to see the array of his elite fourfold army, set out from the city with his infinite army and transport.
Having reviewed the divisions of the army outside the city, that king, who was a proponent of debate, [proceeded].
His mind agitated by the curiosity of floating amidst the talk of Lokāyata sophists and wranglers, bold and yawning, he looked toward the sun and addressed his ministers:

“There is still much time left in the day; what shall we do? Let us enter the city right now and see if there is anyone wise—a recluse or a brahmin—who is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, and who has even attained the state of an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“Let us challenge him; whoever among us is able to converse with him and dispel his doubts, let us approach him and ask questions, and we shall dispel our own doubts.
When this was said, the five hundred Yonakas spoke thus to King Milinda:
“There are, Great King, six teachers: Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, Ajita Kesakambala, and Pakudha Kaccāyana.
They have assemblies, they have followings, they are leaders of groups, well-known, famous, founders of sects, and esteemed as holy men by the multitude. Go, Great King, and ask them this question.”
“Ask what you wish; let your doubt be dispelled.
Then King Milinda, surrounded by five hundred Yonakas, mounted his excellent chariot Bhadravāhana and approached Pūraṇa Kassapa.
Having approached him, he exchanged greetings with Pūraṇa Kassapa.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Milinda said this to Pūraṇa Kassapa:
“Venerable Kassapa, who protects the world?”
“Great King, the earth protects the world.
“If, venerable Kassapa, the earth protects the world, then why is it that beings going to the Avīci hell pass beyond the earth?
When this was said, Pūraṇa Kassapa was unable to swallow it down, nor was he able to spit it out; with his head bowed and shoulders slumped, he sat silent and brooding.
Then King Milinda said this to Makkhali Gosāla:
“Venerable Gosāla, are there wholesome and unwholesome kamma-s? Is there a fruit and result of well-done and ill-done kamma-s?
“There is no such thing, Great King, as wholesome and unwholesome kamma-s; there is no fruit or result of well-done and ill-done kamma-s.”
"Great King, those who are kṣatriyas here in this world will, having gone to the next world,
become kṣatriyas once again; those who are brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas will, having gone to the next world,
likewise become brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas once again."
“What is the use of wholesome and unwholesome kamma?
“If, venerable Gosāla, those here in this world who are kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas,
upon going to the next world, will again become kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas, [then what is the use of wholesome and unwholesome kamma?]”
"There is nothing to be done by means of wholesome or unwholesome kamma.
Therefore, venerable Gosāla, those in this world whose hands have been cut off will, having gone to the next world, likewise have their hands cut off;
those whose feet have been cut off will likewise have their feet cut off."
Those whose hands and feet were cut off will remain with their hands and feet cut off;
those whose ears were cut off will remain with their ears cut off;
those whose noses were cut off will remain with their noses cut off.
“Those whose ears and noses have been cut off shall remain with their ears and noses cut off.
When this was said, Gosāla became silent.
Then it occurred to King Milinda:
“Empty indeed is Jambudvīpa! Vain indeed is Jambudvīpa! There is no ascetic or brahmin capable of conversing with me or dispelling my doubts.
Then King Milinda addressed his ministers:
“How delightful is this moonlit night! To which ascetic or brahmin might we now approach to ask a question? Who is capable of conversing with me and dispelling my doubts?”
When this was said, the ministers stood silent, looking at the face of the king.
Now at that time, the city of Sāgala had been empty for twelve years of recluses, brahmins, householders, and wise men;
so when the king heard that there were places where recluses, brahmins, householders, and wise men were dwelling, he went there to them.
They ask questions, and being unable to satisfy the king with their answers to those questions, they all depart hither and thither.
Those who do not depart for another direction all remain silent.
But the bhikkhus, for the most part, go only to the Himālaya.
Now at that time, one hundred million arahants were residing on the protected plateau of the Himavat mountain.
Then the Venerable Assagutta, having heard King Milinda’s words with his divine ear-element, assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus on the summit of Mount Yugandhara and asked the bhikkhus:
"Is there, friends, any bhikkhu capable of conversing with King Milinda and dispelling his doubts?"
When this was said, the one hundred million arahants became silent.
A second time...
and a third time they were asked, and they remained silent.
Then the Venerable Assagutta said this to the community of monks:
"Friends, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, to the east of the Vejayanta Palace, there is a celestial mansion named Ketumatī;
there dwells a son of the gods named Mahāsena, who is capable of conversing with King Milinda and dispelling his doubts."
Then, a hundred million arahants, having vanished from Mount Yugandhara, appeared in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Sakka, lord of the devas, saw those bhikkhus coming from afar;
having seen them, he approached the Venerable Assagutta, and having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Assagutta, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Venerable Assagutta:
"Venerable sir, a great community of monks has arrived; I am the monastery attendant for the Saṅgha. What is needed?
What should I do? Then the Venerable Assagutta said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“Great King, in the city of Sāgala in Jambudīpa, there is a king named Milinda, a sophist who is difficult to approach and difficult to overcome;
he is declared to be the foremost among many founders of various sects. Having approached the community of monks, he torments the community of monks by asking questions based on dogmatic views.”
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Venerable Assagutta:
"Venerable sir, this King Milinda has passed away from here and been reborn among humans.
Venerable sir, there dwells in the Ketumatī mansion a son of the devas named Mahāsena; he is capable of conversing with that King Milinda."
“Let us dispel his doubt; we shall entreat that son of the gods to be reborn in the human world.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, placing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in front, entered the Ketumatī mansion, embraced the son of the gods Mahāsena, and said this:
“The Saṅgha of bhikkhus, dear sir, entreats you to be reborn in the human world.”

“Venerable sir, I have no need for the human world with its abundance of kamma; the human world is oppressive. Right here, venerable sir, in the world of the gods, having attained higher and higher rebirths, I shall attain final nibbāna.
A second time… and a third time, when Sakka, lord of the devas, made his request, the deva-son Mahāsena spoke thus:

“Venerable sir, I have no concern with the human world, which is full of kamma; the human world is distressing. Right here, venerable sir, in the world of the gods, having attained higher and higher rebirths, I shall attain final Nibbāna.
Then the Venerable Assagutta said this to the deva-son Mahāsena:
“In this world, dear sir, as we survey the world together with its devas, we see none other than you [who can answer] King Milinda.”
“We see no one else capable of refuting his arguments and upholding the Dispensation.

Therefore, dear sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus entreats you: ‘It would be well, O good man, if you were to be reborn in the human world and uphold the Dispensation of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
When this was said, the deva-son Mahāsena thought, “I am indeed to refute the arguments of King Milinda and uphold the Buddha’s Dispensation...”
“I shall be capable of exerting myself,” he thought, and becoming exceedingly joyful and elated, he gave his promise, saying, “Excellent, venerable sirs!
I shall arise in the world of humans.
Then those bhikkhus, having completed their business in the world of the gods, vanished from among the Tāvatiṃsa devas and appeared on the protected plateau of the Himavat mountains.
Then the Venerable Assagutta said this to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
“Venerable friends, is there any bhikkhu in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus who has not come to the assembly?
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Venerable Assagutta:
“Venerable sir, there is the venerable Rohaṇa; on the seventh day from now, having entered the Himavat mountains, he has attained cessation (nirodha). You should send a messenger to his presence.

At that very moment, the venerable Rohaṇa emerged from cessation, thinking, “The Saṅgha is waiting for me,” and vanished from the Himavat mountains to appear before a hundred million arahants at Rakkhitatala.
Then the venerable Assagutta said this to the venerable Rohaṇa:
“Friend Rohaṇa, when the Buddha’s dispensation was being split, did you not see the duties to be performed for the Saṅgha?
“I was not paying attention, venerable sir.
“In that case, friend Rohaṇa, perform a penance.”
“What shall I do, venerable sir?
“There is, friend Rohaṇa, on the slopes of the Himalayan mountains a brahmin village named Gajaṅgala;
there dwells a brahmin named Soṇuttara, and to him a son will be born named the boy Nāgasena. Therefore—”
“Friend Rohaṇa, having entered that family for alms for seven years and ten months, bring forth the boy Nāgasena and ordain him;
once he has been ordained, you will be released from the disciplinary penalty.
Venerable Rohaṇa replied, “Very well.”
He accepted it.
Then the young deva Mahāsena, passing away from the world of the gods, took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin Soṇuttara’s wife;
and together with his taking of rebirth, three wonderful and marvelous phenomena appeared.
The weapons and implements burst into flame, the finest grain was produced, and a great rain fell from the clouds. Yet,
from the time of his conception until seven years and ten months later,
while entering that family for alms, the Venerable Rohaṇa did not receive even on a single day so much as a spoonful of rice or a ladleful of gruel.
He received neither a greeting, nor a salutation with joined palms, nor the performance of respectful duties; instead, he received only abuse and insults.
There was not even a single word spoken to him such as, "Pass by, venerable sir.
However, after the lapse of seven years and ten months, one day [someone said], "Pass by, venerable sir."
He received only a word of greeting.
On that very day, as the brahmin was returning from his work outside, he saw the Elder on the path and asked, "Have you been to our house, sir, O renunciant?
"Yes, brahmin, we went," he replied.
“Did you receive anything? “Yes, brahmin, we did.
Displeased, he went home and asked:
“Did we give anything to that one who had gone forth?
“We gave him nothing.
On the second day, the brahmin sat right at the door of his house, thinking, “Today I will refute the one who has gone forth with a falsehood.”
On the second day, the Elder arrived at the door of the brahmin’s house.
Upon seeing the Elder, the brahmin said this:
“Yesterday, you came to our house and, having received nothing at all, said, ‘We have received. Is such lying permissible for you?”
The Elder said:
“Brahmin, for seven years and ten months we have not received even the mere words ‘Please wait’ from you in your house;
yet yesterday we received the mere words ‘Please wait,’ and so this verbal exchange has been restored.”
“...having taken [this] as a basis, we have spoken thus.
The brahmin thought:
“Having obtained even this much verbal reciprocity, they praise themselves in the midst of people, saying, ‘We have gained [something]. What else...”
Having gained confidence, he thought, "Why do they not praise [this] after receiving some solid or soft food?
He then had a ladleful of alms-food and suitable curry given from the meal prepared for himself,
saying, "You shall receive this alms-food at all times."
He said:

From the following day onwards, seeing the tranquility of the Elder as he approached, the layman became even more confident in his faith and requested that the Elder come to his own house every day for his meal.
The Elder consented by remaining silent; thus, after performing his meal duties day after day, he would depart while reciting small portions of the Buddha’s word as he went.
And that brahmin woman, at the end of ten months, gave birth to a son; they gave him the name Nāgasena. As he grew up in due course, he reached the age of seven years.
Then the father of the boy Nāgasena said this to him:
"My dear Nāgasena, you should train in the sciences within this brahmin family."
“What, dear father, are the ‘trainings’ in this brahmin family?
“The three Vedas, dear Nāgasena, are called the trainings; all other crafts are simply called crafts.
“In that case, dear father, I shall undergo training.”

Then the brahmin Soṇuttara, having given a thousand [pieces of money] as the teacher’s fee to the brahmin teacher, prepared a single couch together in one chamber within the palace and said this to the brahmin teacher:
“Brahmin, please have this boy recite the mantras.
“In that case, dear boy, learn the mantras.”

The Brahmin teacher recited [the texts], and by a single lesson alone, the three Vedas became fixed in the heart, mastered in speech, well-retained, well-determined, and well-attended to by the boy Nāgasena; at once, insight arose in him regarding the three Vedas, together with the Nighaṇṭus and Keta-bhas,
the analysis of phonemes, and the Itihāsa as the fifth— [making him] a master of words and grammar.
He was proficient in the Lokāyata system and the marks of a Great Man.
Then the boy Nāgasena said this to his father:
"Father, are there any further things to be studied beyond these in this brahmin family, or is it only this much?"
“There are no further subjects to be studied in this brahmin family, dear Nāgasena; only these many things need to be learned.
Then the boy Nāgasena, having given his teacher his leave, descended from the palace.

Stirred in his heart by his former mental impressions (*pubbavāsanā*), he went into seclusion and, reflecting upon the beginning, middle, and end of his own craft, [found] at the beginning or in the middle...

Or, having seen not even the slightest essence at the beginning or at the end, he became remorseful and dissatisfied, thinking: "Alas, these Vedas are empty! Alas, these Vedas are mere chaff, without essence and devoid of substance!"
Now at that time, the Venerable Rohaṇa, while seated in the Vattaniya lodging,
having understood with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the boy Nāgasena, dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, vanished from the Vattaniya lodging,
and appeared in front of the brahmin village of Gajaṅgala.

The boy Nāgasena saw the Venerable Rohaṇa approaching from afar while he was standing at his own gatehouse. Upon seeing him, he became joyful, elated, glad, and filled with rapture and happiness, thinking:
"Perhaps this renunciant might know some essential truth.
He went to where the Venerable Rohaṇa was, and having approached, he spoke thus to the Venerable Rohaṇa:
“Who are you, dear sir, who are thus clothed in shaven hair and saffron robes?
“I am one who has gone forth, children.
“By what means, dear sir, have you gone forth?”
“I drive away evil stains; therefore, child, I am called ‘one who has gone forth’ (pabbajita).
“For what reason, dear sir, are your hair and beard not like those of others?
“Child, having seen these sixteen obstacles, I shaved off my hair and beard and went forth.”
“What are the sixteen? “The impediment of ornaments, the impediment of beautification, the impediment of anointing with oil, the impediment of bathing, the impediment of garlands,
the impediment of perfumes, the impediment of unguents, the impediment of myrobalan fruit, the impediment of emblic myrobalan fruit, and the impediment of dye.”
“The impediment of marriage, the impediment of shaving the head, the impediment of the barber, the impediment of disentangling the hair, and the impediment of lice.
When their hair is shaved off, people grieve, suffer, lament, beat their breasts, weep, and fall into confusion.
It is because they are shrouded by these sixteen impediments, young man, that people lose all the most subtle crafts.”
“For what reason, dear sir, do you not have clothes like those of others?
“Clothes, young man, are dependent on sensual pleasures; the accoutrements and ornaments of a householder are dependent on sensual pleasures.
Whatever fears arise from clothing do not exist for one who wears the saffron robe. Therefore, as for clothes...”
“Not as [the skills] of others.
“Do you know, dear sir, what are called the crafts?
“Yes, child, I know the crafts; I even know that spell which is supreme in the world.”
“Is it possible for me also to give that, dear sir?
“Yes, child, it is possible.
“Then give it to me.”
“It is not the right time, young man, for we have entered among the houses for alms.

Then the boy Nāgasena took the bowl from the Venerable Rohaṇa’s hand, led him into the house, and with his own hands served and satisfied him with various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft; and having so done, he [addressed] the Venerable Rohaṇa...
When he had finished eating and had removed his hand from the bowl, he said this:
“Now give it to me, dear sir, the charm. He replied:
“Child, when you have become free from obstacles and, having obtained your parents’ permission, take up the ascetic garb donned by me, then I will give it to you. Thus he spoke.
Then the boy Nāgasena approached his parents and said:
"Mother and father, this renunciant says, 'I know that mantra which is supreme in the world,' yet he does not give it to anyone who has not gone forth in his presence.
I shall go forth in his presence and learn that supreme mantra."
Then his parents, thinking, "Even though he has gone forth, let our son learn the mantras; having learned them, he will return again," gave their permission, saying, "Learn them, my son.
Thereupon the Venerable Rohaṇa, taking the boy Nāgasena with him, went to the Vattaniya monastery and to Vijambhavatthu.
Having arrived, he stayed for one night at the monastery in Vijambhavatthu and then proceeded to Rakkhitatala.
He approached him; having approached, he had the boy Nāgasena ordained in the midst of one hundred million arahants.
Once ordained, the Venerable Nāgasena said this to the Venerable Rohaṇa:
"Venerable sir, I have taken on your appearance; now give me the secret mantra."
Then the Venerable Rohaṇa thought, "In what field should I first instruct Nāgasena—the Vinaya, the Suttanta, or the Abhidhamma?
Having reflected, he considered, "This Nāgasena is wise; he is able to master the Abhidhamma with ease," and so he instructed him first in the Abhidhamma.
And the Venerable Nāgasena [began] with "wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states"—an exposition adorned with the triplets and couplets.
The *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-pakaraṇa*; the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*, adorned with the eighteen Vibhaṅgas beginning with the *Khandhavibhaṅga*;
the *Dhātukathā-pakaraṇa*, analyzed in fourteen ways beginning with "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) and "non-inclusion" (*asaṅgaha*);

the *Puggalapaññatti-pakaraṇa*, analyzed in six ways beginning with "the designation of aggregates" (*khandhapaññatti*) and "the designation of bases" (*āyatanapaññatti*); [and] within its own school...
The *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa* is analyzed by combining one thousand suttas—five hundred suttas concerning our own doctrine and five hundred suttas concerning the doctrines of others;
the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa* is analyzed in ten ways, beginning with "Root Yamaka" and "Aggregates Yamaka";
and [the *Paṭṭhāna*] is analyzed in twenty-four ways, beginning with "Root-condition," "Object-condition," and so forth.

Regarding the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa*: having made the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka proficient through a single recitation, he said, "Wait, venerable sirs, do not recite further; I shall master it with this much alone.
Then the Venerable Nāgasena approached the one million arahants; having approached them, he spoke thus to the one million arahants:
“Venerable sir, having categorized it within these three headings—‘wholesome states,’ ‘unwholesome states,’ and ‘indeterminate states’—I shall set forth that entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka in detail.
“Very well, Nāgasena, set it forth,” [the King said].
Then the Venerable Nāgasena set forth the seven treatises in detail over the course of seven months; the earth...
There was a great roar; the deities gave shouts of approval, the Brahmās clapped their hands, and celestial sandalwood powder and celestial mandārava flowers rained down.
Then, one hundred times ten million arahants conferred full ordination upon the Venerable Nāgasena, who was twenty years of age, on the protected terrace.

And when the Venerable Nāgasena had been ordained, at the end of that night, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, as he was entering the village for alms together with his preceptor, he gave rise to this reflection:
"Empty indeed is my preceptor; foolish indeed is my preceptor, for he has set aside the rest of the Buddha’s word."
“First you trained me in the Abhidhamma.
Then the Venerable Rohaṇa, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Venerable Nāgasena’s mind, said to the Venerable Nāgasena:
“Nāgasena, you have reflected on an inappropriate thought; this is not worthy of you, Nāgasena.”
Then it occurred to the Venerable Nāgasena:
"How wonderful, how marvelous! That my preceptor should know the reflection in my mind with his own mind! My preceptor is truly wise; what if I were now to ask my preceptor's forgiveness?
Then the Venerable Nāgasena said this to the Venerable Rohaṇa:
“Forgive me, venerable sir; I shall not think such thoughts again.
Then the Venerable Rohaṇa said this to the Venerable Nāgasena: “I do not yet forgive you for that much alone, Nāgasena.
There is a city named Sāgala, and there a king named Milinda rules.”
“He causes [this] to be done; having asked questions by way of his own philosophical tenets, he harasses the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
If you go there and, having subdued that king, inspire him with confidence in the Buddha’s teaching, then I shall forgive you.
“Let alone one King Milinda, Bhante;”
“Venerable sir, if all the kings in the entire land of Jambudīpa were to come and ask me questions, I would answer them all and remain composed.
But if, after I have said, ‘Venerable sir, forgive me,’ he should reply, ‘I do not forgive you,’ then, venerable sir, in whose presence shall I dwell for these three months? he asked.
“Nāgasena, this venerable Assagutta is staying at the Vattaniya monastery. Go, Nāgasena, approach the venerable Assagutta;
having approached him, pay homage with your head at the feet of the venerable Assagutta in my name, and say this to him:
‘Venerable sir, my preceptor pays homage with his head at your feet.’”
He pays homage and asks after your health, freedom from illness, physical lightness, strength, and well-being, saying:
"Venerable sir, my preceptor has sent me to stay in your presence for these three months. When asked, "What is the name of your preceptor?
you should say, "Venerable sir, his name is Thera Rohaṇa. When asked, "And what is my name? you should say thus:
“Venerable sir, my preceptor knows your name.

“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Nāgasena replied. Then, having paid homage to the Venerable Rohaṇa and circumambulated him, he took his bowl and robe and, wandering by stages on his alms-tour, arrived at the Vattaniya monastery where the Venerable [Mahā-Kaccāna] was staying.
He approached the Venerable Assagutta; having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Assagutta, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Venerable Nāgasena said this to the Venerable Assagutta:
"Venerable sir, my preceptor pays homage with his head at your feet and says this: 'May you be free from illness and free from affliction...'"
“He asks after your health, strength, and comfortable living, and says: ‘Venerable sir, my preceptor has sent me to stay in your presence for these three months.
Then the Venerable Assagutta said this to the Venerable Nāgasena:
“What is your name?
“Venerable sir, my name is Nāgasena.
“What is the name of your preceptor?”
“My preceptor, venerable sir, is named Rohaṇa.
“What is my name? “My preceptor, venerable sir, knows your name.”
“Excellent, Nāgasena! Put away your bowl and robes.
“Very well, venerable sir,” he replied, and having put away his bowl and robes, on the following day he swept the courtyard and prepared water for washing the face and a tooth-stick.
The Elder swept the place that had been swept, threw away that water, and brought other water; and that too—
Having removed his tooth-stick, he took another tooth-stick and did not engage in conversation;
having done this for seven days, on the seventh day he asked again, and when the Venerable had spoken in the same manner once more, [the king] granted him permission to enter the rains retreat.
Now at that time, a certain great female lay follower had been attending upon the Venerable Assagutta for thirty years.
Then, at the end of three months, that great female lay follower approached the Venerable Assagutta; having approached, she said this to the Venerable Assagutta:
"Is there, dear sir, any other monk in your presence?
"There is, great female lay follower; there is a monk in our presence named Nāgasena."
“Therefore, dear Assagutta, please accept tomorrow’s meal together with Nāgasena.
The Venerable Assagutta consented by remaining silent.
Then, at the end of that night, in the morning, the Venerable Assagutta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and departed.
Accompanied by the Venerable Nāgasena as his attendant monk, he approached the residence of the Great Laywoman;
having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the Great Laywoman, with her own hands, personally satisfied and served the Venerable Assagutta and the Venerable Nāgasena with choice hard foods and soft foods.
Then, when the Venerable Nāgasena had finished his meal and had put away his bowl, the Venerable Assagutta said to him:
“Nāgasena, offer words of thanksgiving for the meal to the Great Laywoman. Having said this, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then the Great Laywoman said to the Venerable Nāgasena:
“Venerable Nāgasena, I am old; please offer me a blessing following this profound discourse on the Dhamma.
Then the Venerable Nāgasena offered a blessing for that great female lay follower’s profound discourse on the Dhamma, which was supramundane and connected with emptiness.
And at that very seat, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in that great female lay follower.
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.

Then the Venerable Nāgasena, having offered his thanks to that great female lay follower, reflected upon the Dhamma he had taught himself; establishing insight while still seated on that very seat, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then the Venerable Assagutta, sitting in the assembly hall, became aware of the attainment of the Eye of Dhamma by both of them.
He uttered a cry of approval, saying, “Excellent, excellent, Nāgasena! With a single discharge of an arrow, two great bodies have been split asunder.
And many thousands of deities likewise uttered cries of approval.
Then the Venerable Nāgasena rose from his seat and approached the Venerable Assagutta; having approached him, he...
Having paid homage to the Venerable Assagutta, he sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Nāgasena was sitting there, the Venerable Assagutta said this to him:
“Go, Nāgasena, to Pāṭaliputta. In the city of Pāṭaliputta, the Venerable Dhammarakkhita resides in the Asoka Monastery; learn the word of the Buddha from him.”
“How far from here, venerable sir, is the city of Pāṭaliputta?
“It is several hundred yojanas away, Nāgasena.
“The road, venerable sir, is indeed long.”
“Alms will be difficult to obtain on the way; how shall I go?
“Go, Nāgasena; you will receive almsfood on the way—rice from the fields, free of black grains, with many soups and many condiments.
“Yes, venerable sir,” said the Venerable Nāgasena. He paid homage to the Venerable Assagutta, keeping him to his right, and taking his bowl and robe, set out on a walking tour toward Pāṭaliputta.
Now at that time, a merchant from Pāṭaliputta was traveling along the road leading to the village of Pāṭaliputta with five hundred carts.
The merchant from Pāṭaliputta saw the Venerable Nāgasena coming from afar;
seeing him, he approached the Venerable Nāgasena and, having approached, paid homage to the Venerable Nāgasena.
“Where are you going, dear? he asked.
“To Pāṭaliputta, householder,” he replied.
“Very well, dear; we too shall go to Pāṭaliputta.”
“Come with us in comfort.

Then the merchant of Pāṭaliputta, having gained confidence in the Venerable Nāgasena’s deportment, personally served and satisfied the Venerable Nāgasena with choice hard food and soft food, and having invited him to eat, [said: the Venerable...
When Nāgasena had finished eating and had put away his bowl, the merchant of Pāṭaliputta took a low seat, sat down to one side, and said to the Venerable Nāgasena:
“What is your name, dear sir?”
“I am, householder, Nāgasena by name.
“Do you know, dear sir, what is called the word of the Buddha?
“I know them, householder, the verses of the Abhidhamma.”

“It is a gain for us, dear sir; it is well-gained by us, dear sir! I too, dear sir, am a master of the Abhidhamma, and you too are a master of the Abhidhamma. Speak, dear sir, of the words of the Abhidhamma.
Then the Venerable Nāgasena taught the Abhidhamma to the merchant of Pāṭaliputta. While he was teaching, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in the merchant of Pāṭaliputta:
“Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation.”
Then the merchant of Pāṭaliputta, having sent about five hundred carts ahead and following behind himself, stood at a forked road not far from Pāṭaliputta and said this to the Venerable Nāgasena:
"This, dear Nāgasena, is the path to the Asokārāma;
this, dear sir, is our precious woolen blanket, sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width. Pray accept this precious blanket, dear sir."
“Out of compassion.
And out of compassion, the Venerable Nāgasena accepted that precious woolen blanket.
Then the merchant of Pāṭaliputta, joyful, elated, glad, and filled with rapture and happiness, paid homage to the Venerable Nāgasena, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then the Venerable Nāgasena went to the Asokārāma where the Venerable Dhammarakkhita was;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Dhammarakkhita, he explained the reason for his coming.
In the presence of the Venerable Dhammarakkhita, he mastered the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas according to the letter in a single recitation over the course of three months.
Again, after three months, he attended to it eight times.
Then the Venerable Dhammarakkhita said this to the Venerable Nāgasena:
"Just as, Nāgasena, a cowherd guards the cows while others enjoy the dairy products; [so it is with you]."
"Even so, Nāgasena, though you uphold the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas, you do not partake in the fruit of recluseship.
"Let it be, venerable sir; enough with this much.
On that very day and during that very night, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Together with...
Through the Venerable Nāgasena’s penetration of the Truths, all the devas gave their applause;
the earth resounded, the Brahmās clapped their hands, and celestial sandalwood powder and divine mandārava flowers rained down.

At that time, one hundred koṭis of Arahants, having assembled on the protected plateau of Mount Himavanta, sent a messenger to the Venerable Nāgasena, saying: "Let Nāgasena come; we desire to see Nāgasena."
Then the Venerable Nāgasena, having heard the messenger’s words, vanished from the Asoka Monastery and appeared on the protected plateau of the Himavat mountain before a hundred koṭis of arahants.
Then those hundred koṭis of arahants said this to the Venerable Nāgasena:
“Nāgasena, this King Milinda is harassing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with debate and the posing of questions.”
“Excellent, Nāgasena! Go, tame King Milinda.
“Let it be, venerable sir, that King Milinda alone comes;

if, venerable sir, all the kings in the entire Jambudīpa were to come and ask me questions, I would answer them all and remain composed. Therefore, venerable sir, go fearlessly to the city of Sāgala.”
Then the elder bhikkhus made the city of Sāgala radiant with the yellow robes of the monks and fragrant with the scent of the sages.
At that time, the Venerable Āyupāla was residing in the Saṅkhyeyya Monastery.
Then King Milinda said this to his ministers:

“Ah, how delightful indeed is this moonlit night! To which ascetic or brahmin might we now approach for conversation and to ask questions? Who is capable of conversing with me and dispelling my doubts?
When this was said, the five hundred Yonakas said to King Milinda:
“There is, Great King, an elder named Āyupāla, a master of the Three Piṭakas, learned and well-versed in the Agamas; he is currently residing at the Saṅkhyeyya Monastery.”
“Go, Great King, and ask the Venerable Āyupāla a question.
“In that case, my man, inform the Bhadanta,” he said.
Then the fortune-teller sent a messenger to the presence of the Venerable Āyupāla, saying, “Venerable sir, King Milinda desires to see the Venerable Āyupāla.”
The Venerable Āyupāla also said,
"In that case, let him come.
Then King Milinda, surrounded by about five hundred Yonakas, mounted his excellent chariot and proceeded toward the Saṅkhyeyya Pariveṇa.
He approached the Venerable Āyupāla; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Āyupāla, and after exchanging courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Milinda said this to the Venerable Āyupāla:
“Venerable Āyupāla, for what purpose is your going forth, and what is your ultimate goal?
The elder replied:
“Great King, the purpose of our going forth is the practice of Dhamma and the practice of equanimity; however, the fruit of recluseship is our ultimate goal.”
“But, venerable sir, is there anyone who, though a householder, is a practitioner of the Dhamma and a practitioner of integrity?
“Yes, great king, there are householders who are practitioners of the Dhamma and practitioners of integrity.
Great king, when the Blessed One was setting in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma at Isipatana in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī, there was the realization of the Dhamma for eighteen crores of Brahmās.”

Furthermore, O Great King, when the Blessed One was teaching the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, the Samacittapariyāya Sutta, and the Rāhulovāda Sutta, there occurred an attainment of the Dhamma by deities beyond all calculation; yet all of them were householders, not those who had gone forth.
"While the Parābhava Sutta was being taught, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by devas beyond counting;
yet all of them were householders, not those who had gone forth.

"In that case, venerable Āyupāla, your going forth is useless. It is due to the result of evil karma committed in the past that these ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, go forth and maintain the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas)."
“Venerable Āyupāla, those bhikkhus who eat at a single sitting must surely have been thieves in the past who carried off the wealth of others.
Having plundered the wealth of others, as the result of that karma, they now eat at a single sitting;
they do not obtain [food] to enjoy from time to time. They possess neither virtue, nor asceticism, nor the holy life.”
"But as for those monks, venerable Āyupāla, who live in the open air, surely they were robbers who formerly plundered villages;
having destroyed the houses of others, by the outflow of that karma they now live in the open air, unable to enjoy lodgings. They have no virtue, no austerity, and no holy life."
"But as for those monks, venerable Āyupāla, who remain sitting, surely they were highway-robbers in the past;

having seized, bound, and made others—travelers on the road—sit down, by the result of that karma they have now become those who remain sitting, unable to lie down to rest. They possess neither virtue nor asceticism."
“There is no holy life,” he said.
When this was said, the Venerable Āyupāla remained silent and did not offer any reply.
Then the five hundred Yonakas said this to King Milinda:
“He is wise, Great King, and an elder; yet he is lacking in confidence and says nothing in reply.
Then King Milinda, seeing that the Venerable Āyupāla remained silent, clapped his hands, raised a shout, and said to the Yonakas:
“Empty indeed is Jambudvīpa! Shallow indeed is Jambudvīpa! There is no ascetic or brahmin at all who dares to converse with me or to dispel my doubts!”
Then, as King Milinda surveyed that entire assembly and saw that the Yonakas were neither afraid nor embarrassed, this thought occurred to him:
"Without a doubt, I think there must be some other wise bhikkhu who dares to converse with me, for it is because of him that these Yonakas are not embarrassed.
Then King Milinda said this to the Yonakas:
“Tell me, is there any other wise monk who is able to converse with me and dispel my doubt?
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgasena was surrounded by a company of ascetics;
he was a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned, famous, esteemed as virtuous by many people, wise, competent, intelligent, subtle, discerning, and learned.

He was disciplined, confident, and learned, a master of the Three Piṭakas and a possessor of true knowledge; he possessed penetrating intelligence and had mastered the traditional scriptures. He had attained the analytical knowledges (*patisambhidā*) and maintained the ninefold teaching of the Master.
Having reached perfection in the word of the Conqueror, he was skilled in the penetration of the Dhamma, its meaning, and its exposition;
he possessed inexhaustible and manifold eloquence, was a versatile speaker with beautiful vocal delivery, and was difficult to approach, difficult to overcome, and difficult to surpass.
Difficult to restrain and difficult to ward off, unshakeable like the ocean, immovable like the king of mountains, a renouncer of strife, a dispeller of darkness,
a maker of light, a great speaker, a crusher of the hosts of rival sects, a subduer of those belonging to other religious orders—
he was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, and royal ministers.
A recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; one who has attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of fame;
one who demonstrates the ninefold jewel of the Victor’s teaching to the elders, the wise, and those endowed with attentive hearing;
one who points out the path of Dhamma, bears aloft the lamp of Dhamma, raises high the sacrificial post of Dhamma, and performs sacrifice.
Embracing the sacrifice of Dhamma, raising the banner of Dhamma, hoisting the flag of Dhamma, blowing the conch of Dhamma,
beating the drum of Dhamma, roaring the lion’s roar, thundering the thunder of Indra, and with his sweet-voiced resonance—
encircled by the web of lightning-flashes of supreme knowledge and filled with the waters of compassion— he thoroughly refreshes the entire world with the great cloud of the nectar of Dhamma.
Wandering on tour through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, he eventually arrived at the city of Sāgala.
There, the Venerable Nāgasena was residing in the Saṅkhyeyya Monastery together with eighty thousand bhikkhus.
Regarding this, the ancients have said:
“Learned, a speaker of diverse discourses,
subtle and confident;
timely and skillful— ”
And skilled in ready wit.
Those monks who were masters of the Three Piṭakas,
as well as those who knew the five Nikāyas;
The four classes of devas indeed paid homage to Nāgasena,
who was profound in wisdom and possessed of great intelligence.
Skilled in what is the path and what is not the path,
Nāgasena has attained the supreme goal, confident and fearless.
Surrounded by those monks who were skillful and speakers of truth,
he wandered through villages and market towns.
He approached Sāgalā.
At that time, Nāgasena was dwelling in the Saṅkhyeyya Monastery.
“He speaks among men like a lion on a mountain.
Then Devamantiya said this to King Milinda:
“Come, Great King; there is, Great King,
an elder named Nāgasena, wise, competent, intelligent, disciplined, confident, learned, an eloquent speaker,
possessed of excellent presence of mind, and one who has reached perfection in the analytical knowledges of meaning, phenomena, language, and ingenuity.”
"He is currently residing in the Saṅkhyeyya Pariveṇa; go, Great King, and ask the Venerable Nāgasena a question.
He is capable of conversing with you and dispelling your doubts.
Then, as soon as King Milinda suddenly heard the name "Nāgasena," fear arose within him, trepidation arose, and his hair stood on end.
Then King Milinda said this to Devamantiya:
"Is the venerable monk Nāgasena able to converse with me?

"He is able, Great King, even to converse with Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Pajāpati, Suyāma, Santusita, and the World-protectors, or even with Mahābrahmā, the father of fathers; how much more so, then, with one who has become a human being?"
Then King Milinda said this to Devamantiya:
"In that case, Devamantiya, send a messenger to the presence of the venerable one.
"Very well, Your Majesty," replied Devamantiya, and he sent a messenger to the venerable Nāgasena, saying: "Venerable sir, King Milinda desires to see the venerable one."
The Venerable Nāgasena also said,
"In that case, let him come. Then King Milinda,
surrounded by about five hundred Yonakas, mounted his excellent chariot and, together with a great military force, approached the Saṅkhyeyya Pariveṇa where the Venerable Nāgasena was staying.
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgasena was seated in the assembly hall together with eighty thousand bhikkhus.
King Milinda saw the assembly of the Venerable Nāgasena from afar, and having seen it, he said this to Devamantiya:
“Whose great assembly is this, Devamantiya?”
“Great King, it is the assembly of the Venerable Nāgasena.
Then, as King Milinda saw the assembly of the Venerable Nāgasena from afar, fear arose within him, trepidation arose, and his hair stood on end.
Then King Milinda was like an elephant surrounded by a rhinoceros, like a serpent surrounded by a garuḷa, like a python surrounded by...
Like a jackal surrounded by dogs, like a bear surrounded by wild buffalo, like a frog followed by a snake, like a deer pursued by a tiger,
like a serpent encountered by a snake-charmer, like a rat encountered by a cat, like a piśāca encountered by a spirit-doctor,
like the moon entering the mouth of Rāhu, like a serpent confined within a basket, or like a bird trapped inside a cage.
Like a fish caught in the mouth of a net, like a man who has entered a forest of wild beasts, like a yakṣa guilty before Vessavaṇa,
or like a son of the gods whose life-span is exhausted— frightened, agitated, terrified, stirred with awe, his hair standing on end, dejected, dispirited,
with a wandering mind and a transformed heart— he maintains mindfulness, thinking: "Let not these attendants despise me."
Having approached Devamantiya, he said this:
"Do not, Devamantiya, tell me about the Venerable Nāgasena; I shall know Nāgasena even without being told.
"Very well, Great King, you yourself shall know him," he replied.
Now at that time, Venerable Nāgasena was junior to forty thousand bhikkhus in front of that assembly of bhikkhus, yet senior to forty thousand bhikkhus behind him.
Then King Milinda, surveying the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus— both in front, behind, and in the middle—
beheld Venerable Nāgasena sitting from afar in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Seeing him like a lion with a golden mane—free from fear and terror, free from horripilation, and free from the paralysis of fear—he recognized him by his very demeanor:
"This, indeed, is Nāgasena here.
Then King Milinda said this to Devamantiya:
“This, Devamantiya, is the venerable Nāgasena.
“Yes, Great King, this is indeed Nāgasena; you have recognized Nāgasena well, Great King.
Thereupon the king was delighted, thinking, “I have recognized Nāgasena even without being told.”
Then, as soon as King Milinda saw the Venerable Nāgasena, fear arose within him, trepidation arose, and his hair stood on end.
Therefore it was said:
“Endowed with virtuous conduct...”
Seeing Nāgasena, well-tamed in the highest taming,
the king spoke these words.
Many views have been declared by me,
and many debates have been engaged in;
yet such fear as this never existed before.
Today my fear is as it was for me before.
Without doubt, defeat will be mine today.
Victory belongs to Nāgasena,
for his mind did not waver.
Thus ends the Discourse on External Matters.
